power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective for anxiety disorders, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but the neurobiological mechanisms of change remain unclear.
This systematic review synthesized neuroimaging evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether CBT can be considered a neurobiological intervention.

Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251239465), PubMed, Scopus and PsycInfo were searched for RCTs of CBT in adults with anxiety disorders, depression or OCD-spectrum disorders reporting preand post-treatment neuroimaging.
Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Seventeen RCTs were included (OCD = 5, anxiety disorders = 6, depression = 6), using task-based fMRI (n = 8), resting-state fMRI (n = 6), structural MRI (n = 2) or PET (n = 1).

Changes after CBT involved emotional reactivity regions, prefrontal and frontoparietal control systems and their connectivity, with disorder-specific patterns: reduced threat reactivity in anxiety disorders, altered cognitive control networks in OCD, and altered mood-related, self-referential and reward connectivity in depression.
Neural and clinical change did not always coincide, and comparisons with pharmacotherapy were mixed.
Five studies were at high risk of bias.
These findings provide preliminary support for CBT as a neurobiological intervention, although small samples and heterogeneous protocols limit conclusions.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most empirically supported psychotherapeutic approaches for anxiety disorders, depression and obsessivecompulsive disorder (OCD) (Cuijpers et al., 2023; Hassan Kariri & Almubaddel, 2024), and is recommended as the first-line treatment by the guidelines of international organizations (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2024; World Health Organization, 2023).

text.text: Despite the strong evidence for its effectiveness, the mechanisms through which therapeutic change is achieved remain less well understood.
As early as the late 1990s, it was argued that psychotherapy works through learning and, consequently, through changes in the brain (Kandel, 1998).

text.text: The cognitive models of anxiety and depression describe psychopathology as an imbalance between the increased bottom-up processing of the threat stimulus and the inefficient top-down cognitive control, with CBT acting to reinforce the latter (Clark & Beck, 2010).

text.text: In terms of neurobiology, bottom-up processing involves brain regions related to emotional reactivity such as the amygdala, the insula, and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), while the top-down control relies on prefrontal regions that regulate their activity (Etkin et al., 2011; Ochsner & Gross, 2005).

text.text: According to these models, effective CBT would be expected to reduce emotional reactivity, increase activation in prefrontal regions, and alter the connectivity between them.
Different models of learning suggest different mechanisms through which this change is achieved, mostly through exposure to the threat stimulus.
For example, according to the emotional processing theory, fear activation by exposure and its reduction during the sessions are prerequisites for therapeutic change (Foa & Kozak, 1986).

text.text: In contrast, the inhibitory learning model suggests that this exposure does not modify the original fear memory but creates new, competing learning and the outcome largely depends on the ability to recall this in future circumstances (Craske et al., 2014).

text.text: Neuroimaging data could contribute in distinguishing between the two models, by examining which neurobiological changes are actually associated with clinical improvement.
Recently, an increasing number of studies has investigated the neurobiological changes that follow CBT, and some systematic reviews have attempted to synthesize their findings.

However, the majority of these reviews focus either on a specific disorder or a specific neuroimaging technique, included studies with no comparing arm or excluded studies with no statistically significant results (König et al., 2025; Picó-Pérez et al., 2023; Poli et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2022).

text.text: A review restricted to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that examines different disorders and imaging techniques together can identify which findings are shared across disorders and which are disorderspecific.
It can also examine whether these changes are associated with clinical improvement.

The aim of the present review was to examine whether CBT could be considered as a neurobiological intervention by synthesizing findings from RCTs in adults with anxiety disorders, depression or disorders within the obsessive-compulsive spectrum.

More specifically, the review examined a) which neurobiological changes follow CBT intervention and whether these are different among different disorders, b) if these changes are related to the patients' clinical improvement, c) whether the changes are different than those following pharmaceutical treatment or other types of psychotherapy, and d) if pre-intervention neurobiological indices could predict CBT response.
The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Page et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and meta-analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Page et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The review process included the following steps; formulating the research question, conducting a thorough search of the existing literature, extracting and evaluating relevant data, and, lastly, synthesizing and presenting the findings.
The review was pre-registered in the international registry PROSPERO under the registration number CRD420251239465.
Each study had to meet specific eligibility criteria.
These were defined a priori, and no modifications were made following the pre-registration in PROSPERO.
A prior search of the registry identified no ongoing or completed reviews addressing the same question.
Only RCTs that investigated the effect of CBT on neurobiological and clinical parameters were included.
Study participants had to be adults (≥ 18 years of age) with a clinically confirmed diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, depression, or a disorder that fell under the obsessive-compulsive spectrum.
The diagnosis had to be established based on DSM or ICD criteria, or via a standardized clinical interview (e.g., SCID, MINI) conducted by a qualified clinician.
No criteria were set regarding the demographic characteristics of the studies' samples (e.g. gender or ethnicity) or the severity of the diagnosis.
The therapeutic intervention had to be any form of CBT (individualized or group delivery), and to describe the intervention's protocol (number of sessions, duration, core techniques).
Regarding neurobiological data, studies had to utilize specific neuroimaging methods.
These methods are presented in Table 1.
text.formatted: These methods are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Studies had to be published in the English language by peer-reviewed journals, irrespective of the time of publication.
Table 1.
Neuroimaging techniques used in the included studies and type of information provided

Regarding the criteria of exclusion, these were the following: a) samples including individuals under the age of 18; b) participants without a primary diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, a depressive disorder, or a disorder within the obsessivecompulsive spectrum; c) samples with a primary diagnosis outside the scope of this review (e.g., psychotic or neurocognitive disorders, autism spectrum disorders); d) studies where the intervention's objective was outside the scope of this review (e.g., stress management); e) studies in which CBT could not be isolated as an independent variable (e.g., combined with other interventions).
Additionally, studies lacking a control group, observational studies or case reports, other systematic reviews and metaanalyses or protocols not providing sufficient data were also excluded.
The PubMed, Scopus, and PsycInfo databases were thoroughly searched between 1 and 27 August 2026, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines.

The terms used were "Cognitive behavioral therapy" OR "CBT" AND "neural mechanisms" OR "neuroplasticity" OR "brain function" OR "functional neuroimaging" OR "fMRI" OR "rs-fMRI" OR "structural MRI" OR "PET" OR "DTI" AND "anxiety disorders" OR "generalized anxiety disorder" OR "panic disorder" OR "social anxiety" OR "mood disorders" OR "major depressive disorder" OR "depression" OR "specific phobias" OR "obsessive-compulsive disorder" OR "OCD" OR "OCD spectrum".
AND "randomized controlled trial" OR "RCT".
A similar conceptual structure was used in all databases, adapted to the syntax and available filters of each.
All retrieved records were imported into Zotero, where duplicates were identified and removed using automatic and manual checks.
Titles and abstracts were screened by two reviewers.
Full texts of potentially eligible studies were assessed independently by two reviewers and disagreements were resolved through discussion.
Additionally, a backward search (hand search of reference lists) of included papers was conducted to identify additional studies relevant to the topic.
The data extraction was conducted in a standardized manner to ensure the accuracy and reproducibility of the results, and was performed by two researchers.
A pre-defined extraction form, developed specifically for the purposes of this review, was used for data collection.
The data extracted by each study included the year of publication, sample size and demographic characteristics (where available), as well as the primary diagnosis and the diagnostic method employed.
Regarding the intervention, details were collected on the method that CBT was delivered, the therapeutic protocol applied (number and frequency of the sessions), and the nature of the comparator arm.
Information was extracted regarding the performed neuroimaging techniques, the psychometric assessments (if any) conducted, and the primary findings of each study.

Methodological quality was assessed with the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs (RoB 2) (Sterne et al., 2019), which evaluates the following five domains; a) bias arising from the randomization process, b) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, c) bias due to missing outcome data, d) bias in the measurements of the outcome, and e) bias in the selection of the reported result.

text.text: Each domain can be rated as low risk, with some concerns, or high risk of bias using signaling questions and the tool's algorithm.
These domain-level judgements determine the overall risk-of-bias rating for each study.
Risk of bias was assessed by one and checked by a second reviewer; any uncertainties were resolved through discussion.

text.text: The 17 included studies were published in peer-reviewed journals between 2006 and 2025.

Five studies included participants with a diagnosis within the OCD spectrum, six included participants with an anxiety disorder (specific phobias, social anxiety disorder and panic disorder with or without agoraphobia), and six focused on depression.
In total, the study groups comprised 492 participants and the comparator arms 782 participants.
The weighted mean age of the participants in the CBT interventions was 33.9 years, with one study reporting only the age range (41-44 years).
The mean proportion of females was 57.6%, with one study not reporting the sex distribution of its sample.
In four studies, a proportion of participants in the CBT group were receiving concurrent medication (mean across these studies 60.5%).
Six studies compared CBT with pharmacotherapy (fluoxetine, escitalopram, escitalopram/duloxetine, or unspecified SSRIs/SNRIs).
Regarding the neuroimaging techniques, eight studies used task-based fMRI, six used resting-state fMRI, two used structural MRI, and one used PET.
With respect to comparison conditions, nine studies used a waitlist control, six used active pharmacotherapy, and two used supportive psychotherapy.
Eight studies employed a three-group design, comprising a CBT group, a clinical control group (waitlist or active treatment), and a healthy control group for comparison of neuroimaging data.
Regarding the CBT protocol, three studies delivered group CBT and 14 delivered individual CBT.
One study used computer-assisted CBT, combining five individual sessions with a nine-module online self-help program.
Three studies were explicitly based on an exposure and response prevention (ERP) protocol.
The number of sessions ranged from one to 20.
Lastly, session duration was approximately one hour for eight of the included studies, whereas the remaining nine used longer sessions, ranging from 90 minutes to 4-5 hours.
The main characteristics of the included studies are presented in detail in Table 2.

text.text: Post-CBT changes clustered in three systems; regions of emotional reactivity (amygdala, insula, ACC), prefrontal cognitive control systems and the default mode network (DMN) and reward circuitry.
The direction of prefrontal changes depended on the performed task.
Activation increased during active emotion regulation (Goldin et al., 2014 (Goldin et al., , 2021) ) and decreased during emotion maintenance (Reinecke et al., 2018).

text.text: This review examined whether CBT can be considered a neurobiological intervention.
Across 17 RCTs, clinical improvement after CBT was accompanied by measurable changes in brain function and connectivity, providing preliminary support for this view.
This is consistent with the long-standing view that psychotherapy, insofar as it is effective, acts through learning and therefore through changes in the brain (Kandel, 1998).
text.formatted: This is consistent with the long-standing view that psychotherapy, insofar as it is effective, acts through learning and therefore through changes in the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kandel, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this view by mapping where such changes occur across disorders.
However, the evidence base is small, heterogeneous and largely correlational, and the findings should be interpreted with necessary caution.

Despite heterogeneity in diagnoses, protocols and imaging methods, most studies reported changes in regions involved in emotional reactivity (amygdala, insula, ACC), in prefrontal and frontoparietal control systems, or in the connectivity between them.

This pattern is broadly consistent with cognitive models of anxiety and depression, which posit an imbalance between increased bottom-up threat processing and insufficient top-down cognitive control (Clark & Beck, 2010), and with the neuroscience of emotion regulation, in which cognitive reappraisal relies on prefrontal modulation of the amygdala (Ochsner & Gross, 2005).

text.text: However, the direction of prefrontal changes varied with the task paradigm, so the data do not support a simple model in which CBT uniformly strengthens prefrontal control.
The pattern was expressed differently in each disorder.

In anxiety disorders, the most consistent finding was reduced reactivity to threat-related stimuli in regions that detect threat and generate bodily arousal (Liebscher et al., 2016; Reinecke et al., 2018; Schienle et al., 2007; Straube et al., 2006).

text.text: In OCD, changes involved networks rather than single regions, including circuits supporting motor and habit control and networks supporting cognitive control.
Notably, the change in cognitive control connectivity was associated with improved resistance to compulsions (Moody et al., 2017), the core target of ERP.

text.text: This suggests that the neural changes accompanying ERP may relate less to the reduction of obsessions than to the capacity to tolerate the urge without acting on it, the component directly trained by response prevention.

In depression, changes involved the relationship between regions linked to negative mood, the network supporting self-focused thought and the cognitive control network (Sheline et al., 2025), as well as connectivity between frontal regions and the reward system (Katayama et al., 2023).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that the neural changes accompanying CBT may involve circuits implicated in the maintenance of each disorder, rather than a nonspecific reduction in brain activity.
As this conclusion derives from small samples, it cannot inform how treatment should be individualized.
The clearest mechanistic signal concerned exposure.
Emotional processing theory proposes that fear activation during exposure is a prerequisite for change (Foa & Kozak, 1986).

text.text: In OCD, however, how strongly the brain's threat-detection system responded during fear learning was unrelated to symptom improvement.
Instead, improvement was associated with lower activity in a parietal region involved in executive control when patients later recalled what they had learned during extinction (Jacoby et al., 2025).

text.text: This finding is consistent with the inhibitory learning model, according to which exposure does not erase the original fear memory but creates a competing safety memory, and outcome depends on whether this new learning is retrieved when the feared stimulus is encountered again (Craske et al., 2014).

text.text: Although based on a single small study using a laboratory task, it is in line with the clinical shift from emphasizing fear reduction within sessions to promoting the retrieval of new learning across different contexts.

In practice, this framework favors strategies such as designing exposures to violate patients' specific expectancies, conducting exposure across varied stimuli and contexts, including between-session practice without the therapist as a safety signal, and evaluating progress by what patients learned rather than by how much their distress decreased within a session (Craske et al., 2014).

text.text: In social anxiety disorder, CBT increased activity in regions involved in attention and emotion regulation and decreased activity in regions involved in processing social cues, such as facial expressions and voices, during exposure to social criticism.

These changes explained a substantial proportion of symptom improvement (Goldin et al., 2014), suggesting that the effects of cognitive restructuring extend beyond how patients verbally reinterpret a situation to how the brain processes social threat.

text.text: In depression, CBT strengthened communication between frontal control regions and a key hub of the reward system, and this was associated with fewer negative automatic thoughts and lower depression severity up to a year after treatment (Katayama et al., 2023).

text.text: Because anhedonia was not assessed, whether CBT acts on reward processing remains a hypothesis for future research.
A central question is whether the observed changes reflect CBT-specific techniques or factors common to other effective psychotherapies.

In the only study comparing CBT with an equally structured active intervention, group CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy resulted in equivalent clinical improvement and increases in cognitive control activation (Goldin et al., 2021).

text.text: Two interventions with different rationales, one targeting the content of thoughts and the other the person's relationship to them, thus converged on the same neural outcome.
This may indicate a common pathway of therapeutic change that can be reached by different routes.

Alternatively, part of the changes attributed to CBT may reflect common factors such as the therapeutic alliance, expectations and psychotherapy structure, which account for a substantial proportion of outcome variance (Wampold, 2015).

text.text: By contrast, when CBT was compared with unstructured supportive therapy, it produced activation and connectivity changes that were not observed in the control group, suggesting that at least some of these changes may be attributable to CBT-specific techniques rather than to common factors (Katayama et al., 2022 (Katayama et al., , 2023)).

text.text: Similarly, in panic disorder, amygdala activation decreased comparably whether exposure exercises were guided by the therapist or carried out by patients alone (Liebscher et al., 2016), suggesting that this change was linked to exposure itself rather than to the therapist's presence during it.

text.text: The present evidence cannot fully distinguish between these accounts, as most studies used waitlist controls, and none measured therapeutic alliance, therapist competence or patient engagement.
Studies comparing CBT with medication can show whether CBT has a distinct neural signature or whether its effects simply accompany symptom reduction.
The evidence is mixed.
In OCD, the volume of the putamen, a structure involved in habit formation, increased only with fluoxetine, despite comparable clinical improvement (Hoexter et al., 2012).

text.text: These findings are compatible with the proposal that psychotherapy acts predominantly top-down, through prefrontal control regions, and pharmacotherapy bottom-up, through deeper emotional regions (DeRubeis et al., 2008; Goldapple et al., 2004).

text.text: Other findings, however, pointed to shared mechanisms.

Remission was associated with reduced connectivity between regions involved in emotional and attentional processing and motor regions, irrespective of treatment (Dunlop et al., 2023), and higher pre-treatment metabolism in regions linked to negative mood and in regions involved in social perception predicted non-response to both CBT and escitalopram (McGrath et al., 2014).

text.text: Given the small number of comparative studies, it would be premature to conclude that CBT has a distinct neurobiological signature.
A more cautious conclusion would be that both psychotherapy and medication alter brain function, possibly through partly different routes.

Baseline brain measures predicted treatment response in several studies, and in two cases differentially predicted response to CBT versus medication (Dunlop et al., 2017; Hoexter et al., 2013; Reggente et al., 2018).

text.text: However, these were exploratory analyses in small samples, and they do not yet support clinical decision-making, nor do they imply that treatment outcome is biologically predetermined.
Neural and clinical change did not always coincide.

Neural changes occurred without between-group differences in depression severity (Katayama et al., 2022), symptoms improved without structural change (Hoexter et al., 2012), and the most prominent activation changes were not those associated with symptom improvement (Jacoby et al., 2025).

text.text: Neuroimaging should therefore not be treated as an objective validation of psychotherapy, as if clinical improvement were meaningful only when visible on a scan.
Reducing psychological difficulties to neurobiology risks overlooking the psychological and interpersonal processes that are often the most clinically important (Miller, 2010).
text.formatted: Reducing psychological difficulties to neurobiology risks overlooking the psychological and interpersonal processes that are often the most clinically important <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Miller, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For clinicians, this implies that the patient's experience and functioning remain the primary indicators of therapeutic change, with neurobiological findings serving to inform, rather than validate, how that change occurs.
However, as none of the included studies tested mediation, the direction of the relationship between neural and clinical change remains unknown.
This review has several strengths.
It was pre-registered in PROSPERO, with eligibility criteria and methods defined before the search was conducted, which reduces the risk of selective inclusion and reporting.
It was also restricted to RCTs, reducing the risk that neural changes reflect the passage of time, repeated measurement or nonspecific effects.

By including anxiety disorders, depression and OCD, and synthesizing task-based, resting-state, structural and metabolic data, it allowed findings that are shared across disorders to be distinguished from those that are disorder-specific.
Beyond identifying which regions change, it examined whether these changes were associated with clinical improvement and how they compared with pharmacotherapy and other psychotherapies.

Finally, findings were interpreted in relation to the clinical processes targeted in CBT, such as exposure, response prevention and cognitive restructuring, linking neuroimaging evidence to questions directly relevant to psychotherapeutic practice.
Some limitations that concern both the primary studies and this review should also be addressed.
The term CBT covered heterogeneous protocols, from a single 4hour exposure session to 20 sessions, which precludes identifying the components responsible for the observed changes.

Samples were small and largely free of comorbidity, limiting generalizability to clinical practice, and a few studies appear to derive from overlapping samples, so the number of independent samples is smaller than the number of studies.
In four studies, participants received concurrent medication, complicating attribution of changes to CBT.
Few studies included follow-up imaging, and task-based paradigms may not capture the processes that occur during exposure or behavioral experiments within therapy.
Lastly, five studies were at high risk of bias, and almost all lacked a pre-specified analysis plan, a notable concern given the analytic flexibility of neuroimaging data.
Limitations of the review itself include the restriction to peer-reviewed English-language publications, which may have introduced language and publication bias.

The heterogeneity of paradigms and outcomes precluded metaanalysis, and the narrative synthesis relied partly on counting studies with significant findings, which does not account for differences in sample size or effect magnitude.
Grouping findings by region and network involved interpretive judgment and was not pre-specified.

Furthermore, RoB2 was designed for clinical outcomes and does not capture imaging-specific sources of bias, such as region-of-interest (ROI) selection or correction for multiple comparisons, and the certainty of evidence was not formally graded.
This systematic review suggests that CBT could be regarded as a neurobiological intervention.
Clinical improvement in OCD, anxiety disorders and depression was accompanied by measurable changes in brain function and connectivity.

Across disorders, changes involved emotional reactivity regions, prefrontal and frontoparietal control systems and their interactions, with disorder-specific patterns that may relate to the mechanisms maintaining each condition.
Evidence for a neural signature distinct from pharmacotherapy and for clinically useful predictors of response remains preliminary.
These conclusions are limited by small samples, heterogeneous protocols and the risk of bias in several studies.
Future research should shift from asking whether the brain changes with CBT to asking which therapeutic processes change which circuits, and in whom.

This requires dismantling designs that isolate specific components (e.g., exposure versus cognitive restructuring), active control conditions, repeated measurements during treatment to capture when and how change occurs (Kazdin, 2007), formal mediation analyses, and systematic assessment of the therapeutic relationship.

text.text: Both CBT variants led to significant posttreatment reductions in amygdala activation.

Therapist-guided exposure produced a significant reduction in the right amygdala (t = 3.37, p = .011) and a trend in the left (p = .057), whereas nonguided exposure produced a significant reduction in the left amygdala (t = 3.15, p = .043) and a trend in the right (p = .082).

Reduction in right amygdala activation correlated positively with reductions in MI (r = .17, p = .049), ASI (r = .16, p = .061) and anxiety ratings (r = .23, p = .006); reduction in left amygdala activation correlated only with reduction in anxiety ratings (r = .21, p = .011)
